assumptions: The parents' installation company can provide or introduce qualified field delivery at market economics, but it does not guarantee property-manager adoption or confer exclusive distribution.
The business is evaluated as resident-deposit- or third-party-financed and does not place full common-infrastructure capex on the founder's balance sheet.
Residents retain their statutory individual application route; any operator agreement controls only lawfully contracted common assets and services and cannot block that alternative.
No proprietary ownership of session data, allocation software, or cross-building learning is assumed until contracts and measurable performance evidence establish it.
evidence_needed_for_higher_score: A higher score requires Polish counsel and a reviewed contract confirming durable operator rights without restricting residents; at least three completed legacy-building pilots with signed resolutions and deposit-backed residents; measured time from lead to live port, activation density, CAC per building and per active port, founder hours, and manager/installer referral conversion; fully loaded contribution margins including hardware, CSMS, field service, warranty, UDT, insurance, billing, payments, and bad debt; renewal or cohort retention evidence; and proof that a portfolio contract, financing facility, proprietary operating asset, or owned data advantage materially outperforms the existing turnkey alternatives.

factors.name: Core insight
factors.rationale: The second or third charger request can make a building-wide expert study, shared riser, and load allocation more rational than duplicated point solutions, and the statutory building approval interface creates a real coordination wedge. The insight is weakened because that interface is not an exclusive right: qualifying residents retain an individual application and metering route, so coordination value does not itself create operator control.

factors.name: Customer pain and willingness to pay
factors.rationale: Legacy buildings can face genuine delay, engineering work, constrained connection power, and material upgrade costs, which gives residents and managers a reason to coordinate. However, the payer is fragmented between individual residents and common-property decision makers, a complete point in an unprepared block can cost about PLN 15,000 net, and no evidence establishes willingness to add the proposed connection fee, hardware markup, and recurring fee or that enough ready-to-pay residents cluster in one building. This is meaningful but uneven pain with price sensitivity still unknown.

factors.name: Business model and economics
factors.rationale: Setup margin plus recurring metering, billing, and capacity-management revenue can produce a sensible mixed model if residents or finance partners fund hardware. Yet the stated founder-net-worth path depends on 400 buildings averaging 40 active ports, while activation density, time to that density, renewal, CAC, field-service cost, CSMS fees, payment costs, warranty, UDT, insurance, and bad debt are all unproven. Revenue per signed but lightly activated building may be too small for a bespoke association sales and engineering process, and the 24-36 month payback is unsupported.

factors.name: Market and beachhead
factors.rationale: Polish multifamily legacy stock with multiple EV requests is a coherent beachhead, and the BEV fleet is growing. The economically attractive subset is narrower than the headline market: newer stock is increasingly cable-ready, older constrained buildings carry the highest capex and approval friction, and July 2026 registration evidence does not prove near-term multi-resident density. The beachhead is identifiable but its count of buildings with both headroom and several ready buyers is unknown.

factors.name: Competitive position and domination potential
factors.rationale: ChargeWise, Wallbox Polska, and installers already offer much of the turnkey bundle, including installation, dynamic load management, access, tariffs, billing, monitoring, maintenance, and support. Open OCPP compatibility reduces technical lock-in, while statutory individual installation remains a substitute. The founder could become a capable local integrator through family-company access, but the current structure does not show a basis for dominating even a regional segment.

factors.name: Expansion potential
factors.rationale: A proven property-manager relationship could extend across a portfolio and later support upgrade planning, energy services, or adjacent building electrification. Those adjacencies are plausible, but the initial asset does not clearly make them easier to win because the platform, charging hardware, and technical mechanism are supplied by third parties and contracts may be building-specific.

factors.name: Defensibility and durability
factors.rationale: Multi-year service agreements and installed common infrastructure could support retention, but the proposed 7-10 year right has not been shown durable, preferential, or compatible with resident rights. Hardware interoperability, incumbent software, and uncertain ownership of session data prevent a credible technical or data moat. Any durability presently rests on ordinary execution quality and relationships rather than a compounding, founder-owned asset.

factors.name: Strength of advantage
factors.rationale: A single study, coordinated riser, and shared load plan could be more convenient and sometimes cheaper than repeated one-off work. The evidence does not establish a step-change in price, speed, financing, guaranteed capacity, or service relative to existing turnkey vendors, and residents can sometimes choose a directly metered individual charger. The offer is a potentially useful integrator package, not yet a behavior-changing advantage.

factors.name: Timing and momentum
factors.rationale: EV fleet growth, building electrification rules, and increasing charger requests create long-run demand for managed multifamily capacity. Timing is mixed rather than exceptional: new-building pre-cabling erodes the proprietary-riser wedge, recent Polish BEV registration momentum is weak, and the hardest legacy buildings remain gated by scarce capacity and upgrades that dynamic load management cannot remove.

factors.name: Distribution
factors.rationale: Property managers and electrical installers are credible concentrated channels, and the parents' installation company offers an unusually practical pilot route. Conversion still requires resident demand aggregation, expert analysis, an owners' resolution or equivalent authority, and potentially long political procurement cycles. Referral economics, portfolio-level contracting, founder sales hours, and CAC per activated port are unknown, while channel partners can also provide or resell competing systems themselves.

factors.name: Execution and risks
factors.rationale: The founder's analytics strengths and family electrical capability improve feasibility, and an asset-light pilot could fit the capital ceiling. Execution nevertheless spans qualified design, fire and electrical safety, UDT treatment, metering and energy contracts, billing and consumer obligations, hardware maintenance, building governance, financing, and field support. Much of this is partner-delegable, but it is operationally and relationship intensive for a founder remaining in full-time employment.

highest_value_structural_change: Replace the proposed quasi-exclusive concession with a portfolio-level, deposit-gated infrastructure-financing structure: sign a property manager across multiple buildings, proceed only where at least three residents place refundable deposits and the expert report confirms sufficient headroom, have an SPV or finance partner own the shared riser, and grant the operator a durable right to operate that financed asset while preserving residents' statutory alternatives. This would concentrate distribution, make asset ownership rather than legal blockage the control point, and prevent low-density buildings from consuming capital.
main_structural_strength: The offer turns repeated resident requests and scarce building electrical capacity into a persistent common-infrastructure service, and the founder has an unusually credible pilot path through family electrical-installation capability and property-manager introductions.
primary_score_limiter: The claimed control point is not yet ownable in the strong sense required by the thesis: resident access is legally nonexclusive, the long-term building right is unproven, and the technical and billing mechanism is already available from interoperable incumbents, leaving weak defensibility behind costly building-by-building acquisition.
strongest_disconfirming_evidence: Polish rules give qualifying residents an individual consent and dedicated-meter route and can permit progress after management silence in some cases, while ChargeWise and Wallbox Polska already bundle the same condominium billing, access, dynamic-load-management, installation, and support functions. Together these facts contradict both statutory exclusivity and technical uniqueness.
